cards.b:
In the 1950s and 60s, mainly in the USA, political scientists wanted to make the subject a real science, like physics or economics.

Their focus moved from institutions to the behaviour of people: voters, leaders and groups. The roots go back to the Chicago School of the 1920s under Charles Merriam.

David Easton listed eight "intellectual foundation stones" of behaviouralism. Remember them; UPSC loves this list.

  • Regularities: behaviour shows patterns.
  • Verification: claims must be testable.
  • Techniques: use proper research tools.
  • Quantification: measure where possible.
  • Values: keep facts and values separate.
  • Systematisation: theory and research must link.
  • Pure science: understanding before application.
  • Integration: work with other social sciences.

"Real Voters Take Quick Votes, So Politics Improves"

The first V is Verification and the second is Values. Regularities, Verification, Techniques, Quantification, Values, Systematisation, Pure science, Integration.

Easton saw politics as a system. Society sends inputs (demands and support). The system turns them into outputs (decisions and policies). Outputs create feedback, which shapes new inputs.

He defined politics as the "authoritative allocation of values" for a society.

Gabriel Almond: structural-functionalism

Every political system performs the same functions, like interest articulation and rule-making, but through different structures.

Almond and Verba: The Civic Culture (1963)

They studied five countries and found three types of political culture: parochial, subject and participant.

Karl Deutsch

He studied politics as communication, with a "cybernetic" model.

• "Science" without relevance. While scholars counted votes, the US faced the Vietnam War, civil rights protests and race riots. Political science had little to say.
  • Status quo bias. By studying "what is", it quietly accepted the existing order.
  • Value-neutrality is a myth. Choosing what to study is itself a value choice.
  • Western bias. Its models fitted the USA but not new countries like India.

Strikingly, the critique came from Easton himself. In his 1969 presidential address to the American Political Science Association, called "The New Revolution in Political Science", he announced post-behaviouralism.

Its two watchwords were relevance and action. Research should address urgent social problems, and scholars have a duty to act on their knowledge.

• Substance over technique. It is better to be vague about an important issue than precise about a trivial one.
  • Values matter. Scholars should openly discuss values.
  • Engage with crisis. Research must address social crisis.
  • Act. Knowledge brings a responsibility to act.
  • Politicise the profession. Academic bodies should take part in public debates.

No. It gave us survey research, election studies and rigorous methods. In India, the CSDS–Lokniti National Election Studies use these tools to study how Indians vote.

Post-behaviouralism did not reject methods. It said methods must serve meaningful questions. Make this point and you will look balanced.

"Post-behaviouralism is a continuation of behaviouralism, not a rejection of it." Comment.
"Explain Easton's systems analysis and its limitations."

Tip: always mention that the same scholar, Easton, led both movements. Use the systems diagram in your answer; examiners reward neat diagrams.
